content.title: Summary
content.body: Linear is worth evaluating for software teams that want a structured place to plan work, track issues, and coordinate delivery. The key question is whether its workflow fits how your team prioritizes work, handles bugs, plans cycles or releases, reports progress, and connects engineering tasks to product decisions. This page is a buyer-oriented research profile, not a hands-on benchmark. Current ratings, review counts, pricing, and plan-specific capabilities have not been independently verified by PilotStack.

content.title: Who should evaluate it
content.body: Consider a trial if your team wants a focused issue-tracking workflow and is prepared to configure statuses, labels, projects, triage, and reporting around a shared process. Include engineers, product managers, design partners, and whoever owns planning or reporting. Ask each role to complete the same representative tasks and note where the tool matches existing habits or introduces new steps.

content.title: Where it may be a poor fit
content.body: Be cautious if your organization relies on highly customized issue types, elaborate approval chains, strict cross-department permissions, portfolio-level reporting, or workflows that extend well beyond software delivery. These are not automatic disqualifiers, but they need explicit tests. A product that works well for one engineering group may not be the right system of record for every department.

content.title: Workflow fit checklist
content.body: Test creating and triaging an issue, linking it to a project or milestone, assigning ownership, managing dependencies, filtering and saving a view, updating priorities, and producing a report that stakeholders can understand. Check how duplicates, blocked work, recurring tasks, and urgent incidents are handled. If your team uses cycles or sprints, validate the planning and carry-over behavior using a realistic sample rather than relying on a demo.

content.title: Integrations and administration
content.body: List the systems that must exchange information with your issue tracker: source control, chat, design, incident management, identity, and analytics. Confirm each integration's current availability, permissions, synchronization behavior, and plan requirements with official documentation. Test what happens when a linked item changes, an integration is disconnected, or a user loses access. Confirm roles, guest access, audit records, SSO, provisioning, and data export against your security requirements.

content.title: Migration plan
content.body: Before switching, export a representative sample from the current system and map issue types, statuses, labels, users, attachments, comments, links, and custom fields. Test whether timestamps, history, relationships, and permissions are preserved. Identify what cannot be migrated and decide whether it must be archived or retained in the source system. Run a pilot with one team and keep the old tool available until reconciliation is complete.

content.title: Cost and plan verification
content.body: Do not rely on a third-party price copied into a review. Check the vendor's current pricing page and plan documentation for your expected user count, billing term, required features, administration, usage limits, and renewal price. Include migration time, training, integrations, and the cost of running two systems during transition. Record the URL and date checked, and ask the vendor to confirm any material uncertainty in writing.

content.title: How to run a useful trial
content.body: Choose three to five representative workflows and agree on pass/fail criteria before the trial begins. Ask users to complete the tasks without coaching, track friction and workarounds, and inspect the resulting reports. Test access removal, exports, and integration failure as well as the happy path. At the end, compare evidence and total cost with at least one alternative. Keep untested claims marked unknown.

content.title: Evidence and limitations
content.body: PilotStack has not independently collected a user survey or run a controlled product benchmark for this profile. Numeric ratings, review totals, exact pricing, company statistics, and the complete feature matrix are therefore not presented as verified. Use Linear's official documentation for current details and validate important workflows in your own environment before adopting the product.

content.title: Decision criteria for product managers
content.body: Product managers should test whether prioritization, roadmaps, milestones, and stakeholder updates stay connected without creating duplicate sources of truth. Confirm which views can be shared with executives or other departments, how roadmap commitments relate to actual issue status, and whether reports can answer the questions leaders ask. If teams require a portfolio view across multiple products, test that specific workflow and its plan requirements rather than assuming a project list is sufficient.

content.title: Decision criteria for engineering leads
content.body: Engineering leads should validate triage, ownership, dependencies, cycle planning, incident handling, and the connection between issues and code changes. Test the path from incoming bug to assigned work, review, release, and closure. Check whether permissions and notifications create useful accountability without generating noise. For teams with service-level commitments or audit requirements, confirm how records are retained, exported, and reviewed.

content.title: Adoption and ongoing ownership
content.body: Before rollout, decide who owns workspace configuration, naming conventions, status changes, integrations, and onboarding. Document a small set of team conventions so each group does not create incompatible workflows. After launch, review examples of stalled or duplicated work and ask users where the process adds friction. If the tool does not improve the agreed measures, adjust configuration or reconsider the fit rather than assuming adoption will improve automatically.

content.title: Before you commit
content.body: Document the exact plan, integrations, security controls, migration assumptions, and renewal cost used in your decision. Confirm important unknowns with vendor documentation or support. A short evidence-based pilot is more reliable than a generic score or a feature list that has not been tested by your team.

content.title: Keep a record of the trial
content.body: Save test cases, screenshots where appropriate, user feedback, source links, and unresolved questions. This record helps the team explain the decision and repeat the evaluation if pricing or requirements change.

content.title: Data model and workflow conventions
content.body: Before rollout, agree on how teams use statuses, labels, projects, cycles, priorities, and ownership. Test whether the same conventions work for bug triage, roadmap work, support escalations, and cross-team dependencies. Document where teams may customize the workflow and where shared definitions are required for reliable reporting. Without these conventions, teams can create inconsistent data that makes dashboards difficult to interpret.

faqs.question: Is Linear suitable for non-engineering teams?
faqs.answer: It depends on how those teams plan and report work. Test their everyday workflows, permissions, and reporting needs alongside the engineering use case before standardizing on one system.

faqs.question: What should we check before migrating to Linear?
faqs.answer: Test export and import of issues, comments, attachments, labels, relationships, custom fields, timestamps, and permissions. Keep a source-system backup and reconcile a representative sample before full migration.

faqs.question: Are Linear's current price and rating verified here?
faqs.answer: No. PilotStack has not independently verified a current price, rating, or review count for this profile. Confirm current plan details and independent user feedback directly from their sources.

faqs.question: How can we evaluate Linear against alternatives?
faqs.answer: Use the same tasks, team roles, data sample, integration needs, and scoring criteria for every candidate. Record what was tested, total cost, migration effort, and unresolved gaps.

author: PilotStack Editorial Team
learningCurve: Steep — requires dedicated training time for full proficiency
whoShouldUse: Software teams that want issue tracking and product planning in a shared workspace should assess Linear against their delivery process. Teams outside engineering should verify that the model fits their work, and organizations with complex approval or permission needs should test those cases before adoption.
whoShouldNotUse: Test workflow flexibility, custom fields, role permissions, audit needs, reporting, and data export. Migration planning should account for comments, attachments, labels, issue relationships, and history. Confirm which administrative and security controls require a particular plan.
